articles.title: Google and Unity unveil gen-AI game-making platforms, and demonstrate one of them with depressingly rubbish "dream game" Space Corridor
articles.author: Robert Purchese
articles.content:
Google and Unity yesterday announced new generative-AI game-making platforms designed to make and shape games by inputting text prompts. Google's product is called Playground and is available for testing now, if you live in the US, and Unity's product is Unity Spark and is "coming soon".
Their side-by-side announcements are more than coincidence. Google Playground will work with and integrate Unity Spark when "creators" want to "expand their concepts" with "robust, professional-level mechanics, high-fidelity 3D capabilities", Google's Playground blog post said.
Given that, there's a sort of two-tiered approach going on here. Google Playground is the entry level platform, a much more - excuse me while I throw-up on myself - 'vibe-coded' idea origination tool. It's the sort of thing you plug a load of words into the text box, presumably while marvelling at your own creativity and taking lifestyle selfies on a beach somewhere, while Google Playground builds a fairly simple game. Then, when you're happy with it, and AI-prompting a post on LinkedIn about your career change, you can share the game with other Playground users.
Said Google: "Games are one of the most creative forms of expression, and the gaming community keeps growing. But game creation has historically been limited to a select group of people who have technical experience and knowledge of complex game engines. Today, we're introducing Playground, an experimental gaming platform that lets you create, play, and share custom games. Playground lowers the barriers to creation, so bringing game ideas to life can now be as easy as describing it through a few prompts — no coding experience required."
"Asking the AI to reproduce a game that has already been made does not make you [Hideo] Kojima" -Unity's Matt Bromberg
Unity Spark, on the other hand, is a more complicated affair. There are text prompts but they work more as shortcuts or helpers within Unity's more traditional game engine package, so it's not just a 'whack a load of text in, sit back, and create' kind of affair. Indeed, in an interview with Gamefile, Unity boss Matt Bromberg underlined this point, stating that Spark was not about "one-shotting" game development.
"I'm not denigrating folks who are interested in one-shotting things," Bromberg said. "I think there's a level of excitement and enthusiasm about what the technology can do. And maybe that's just a way of people celebrating it." But, he said: "Unity Spark is not going to be for everyone. There are many people who don't have the patience and ambition to make something real.
"Asking the AI to reproduce a game that has already been made does not make you [Hideo] Kojima. It doesn't make you a famous game developer any more than typing the first paragraph of War and Peace into your word processor makes you Tolstoy."
One of the major features of Unity Spark is the ability to co-create games with other people in real-time, and a Unity Spark video showed this in action, with a pair of people - Mari and Theo - making their dream game, Space Corridor. It's a pretty rubbish sci-fi shooter, albeit one that's made quickly, and we see obvious complexity in the engine while it's being made.
Gamefile saw Unity Spark demonstrated live, and apparently it pulled assets from Unity's Store for use. Where Google Playground pulls art and assets from, we don't know - Google didn't say. Gamefile also quizzed Bromberg about the carbon footprint of Spark, which presumably requires a lot of power to build games. Could there be an estimated carbon footprint cost next to requests? "We hadn't considered that," Bromberg replied. "That's something worth considering."
Google's and Unity's AI game-generation platforms haven't, understandably, been received favourably by existing game developers. On Bluesky, Dan Marshall of Size Five Games - creator of the recent point-and-click villain comedy Earth Must Die - described Unity Spark's creation of Space Corridor "as the strongest argument I can think of for keeping game dev out of the pro-AI crowd's hands". In response, someone aptly commented: "They successfully identified that their target market was people with no imagination."
Unity isn't the first game engine to heavily incorporate generative-AI, though. Epic Games revealed a big gen-AI push this summer for its ubiquitous game engine Unreal, incorporating large language model support into its current generation of Unreal, and targeting foundational integration of LLMs for Unreal Engine 6. Even Capcom is evolving its in-house RE Engine "for the AI generation", to incorporate help with coding, QA testing, and more.
articles.summary:
Google and Unity have unveiled new generative AI platforms, Playground and Unity Spark, designed to simplify game development by allowing users to create interactive experiences through text prompts.

### Key Points
- Google Playground is an experimental, entry-level platform currently available for testing in the United States.
- Unity Spark is a more advanced tool that integrates AI as a helper within the traditional Unity game engine environment.
- Google Playground allows users to create and share simple games, with an option to export concepts into Unity Spark for professional-level development.
- Unity Spark features real-time collaborative game creation and utilizes assets directly from the Unity Store.
- The platforms join a growing trend of AI integration in gaming, following similar initiatives from Epic Games for Unreal Engine and Capcom for the RE Engine.

### Why it Matters
These platforms represent a significant shift toward lowering technical barriers for game creation, potentially democratizing development for non-programmers. However, the industry remains divided, as many professional developers express concerns regarding the quality of AI-generated content and the long-term impact on creative craftsmanship.

articles.title: Medical company announces program for 'AI-powered prescriptions' in Utah
articles.author: Mason Leib
articles.content:
Medical company announces program for 'AI-powered prescriptions' in Utah
The company walked through the process in a blog post.
A health care company announced Monday that it has received authorization for a pilot program in Utah allowing artificial intelligence to issue initial prescriptions, including acne treatment.
Nolla Health, which is based in New York City, introduced the program in a blog post announcing the "AI-powered prescriptions," its acne treatment prescription process, which will roll out in three stages.
The company said the pilot is the first in the U.S. authorized by a state regulator to allow AI to issue initial prescriptions, and that it was authorized after working with the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy.
The company says the program is designed to close "the access gap" to healthcare, in this case, by avoiding the appointment wait times and costs associated with visiting a dermatologist.
The company said the Nolla Derm application "will prescribe effective acne treatment from $4.99 a month" and require "no office visit."
The post said Utah residents 18 and older can download the app and begin the process at a discounted rate of $4.99 per month.
After verifying their identity, providing informed consent and filling out an intake questionnaire, patients take a "quick five-angle face scan."
"In about 10--15 minutes, this generates a personalized treatment plan and, if appropriate, an initial prescription," the post said.
The pilot will roll out in three stages with physician involvement in each, according to the company.
In the first stage, which includes the first 100 patients, "two licensed physicians independently review and approve every AI-generated prescription before it reaches the patient."
In the second stage, which will include up to 500 patients, "Nolla Derm issues prescriptions directly, and a physician reviews every case after the fact, at least weekly."
In the third stage of the pilot, a 10% sample of prescriptions each month will be reviewed by a physician. A physician will also review "every case involving an escalation or a side effect."
The company said stages one and two would last at least four and eight weeks, respectively.
"Moving to the next stage requires meeting safety targets, including 95% agreement with physicians and zero serious adverse events, and written approval from the state," the post said.
The post continued, "Patients can message a licensed physician through the app at any time, at no extra cost."
The company said acne treatment was a viable starting point for the technology because it is "well understood, low risk, and backed by decades of clinical evidence."
Editor's note: This story has been corrected to clarify that Nolla Health is based in New York City.
articles.summary:
New York-based Nolla Health has launched a pilot program in Utah, becoming the first U.S. company authorized to use artificial intelligence for issuing initial acne treatment prescriptions.

### Key Points
- The Nolla Derm application allows Utah residents aged 18 and older to receive personalized acne treatment plans and prescriptions after a 15-minute digital intake process.
- The program is authorized by the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy and will roll out in three distinct stages with varying levels of physician oversight.
- Safety protocols require a 95% agreement rate between the AI and human physicians, alongside zero serious adverse events, to progress through the pilot stages.
- Patients can access the service for $4.99 per month, bypassing traditional dermatologist office visits and associated wait times.
- The company selected acne treatment for the pilot due to the condition's low-risk profile and extensive clinical evidence.

### Why it Matters
This pilot represents a significant regulatory milestone in the integration of artificial intelligence into clinical workflows and patient care. By automating routine prescription processes, the program aims to reduce healthcare costs and improve access for patients who face barriers to traditional dermatology services.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse AI files away your friendships, arguments, and secrets
articles.author: Danny Bradbury
articles.content:
If you thought that having companies trawling your social media, browsing history, and TV habits for behavioral clues was bad, sit tight. Meta is just getting started. Its Muse personal AI agent is taking surveillance to the next level.
TIME magazine analyzed the software’s internal instructions and found that it maintains constantly updated dossiers on users and the people they know.
Meta released Muse last month, positioning it as a digital assistant that can handle different parts of your life. It can organize your emails, handle your grocery shopping, and cancel your subscriptions. It is available for free, with paid plans for people who want to do more.
Muse has already been downloaded more than five million times. Its ability to handle mundane online tasks could be bad news for businesses that rely on consumers not canceling their subscriptions. Some people think it will liberate thousands of consumers from low-interest bank accounts.
But Muse won’t just help you stick it to the man; it also is the man.
Have I got some bad Muse for you
You have to let Muse access all your systems before it can help organize them for you. Depending on what you connect and the permissions you grant, that can give it access to your calendar, emails, messages, and other personal information.
In doing so, it accesses data. Lots of it. An analysis by Surfshark late last month put it second only to Meta’s AI chatbot among the apps reviewed, with its App Store disclosures listing collection of 31 of 35 data types.
Those disclosures include Apple’s “Sensitive Info” category, which covers information such as racial or ethnic data, sexual orientation, pregnancy, disability, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, political opinion, genetic information, and biometric data. That doesn’t mean Muse collects every one of those details about every user, but it does show how broad its declared collection can be.
According to TIME’s analysis, Muse’s instructions call for it to refresh personal dossiers every hour. These can record how users met their contacts, along with arguments or tensions within social groups.
Somehow even creepier than that is its nightly review of your recent conversations, which it uses to guide future conversations. For example, it learns when a quick nudge for your attention will be most successful.
Meta uses Muse interactions to train its AI models by default, unless you opt out in the app’s settings.
Oh, and Muse stores these files in Meta’s cloud, where Meta can access them. The company says it will offer encryption that keeps them private even from Meta, but that option isn’t available yet, according to TIME.
Meta says Muse’s conversations and stored data are not shared with its advertising systems. It also says users choose how much access Muse gets and can tell it to forget specific things it has learned.
The magazine points out that simply not using Muse might not save you, because Muse can collect data on people that its users interact with. If you send a Muse user a message and the AI has access to that messaging system, your message can become part of what it reads.
Privacy nonprofit the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC) points out that Meta has pulled a similar trick before, by building shadow profiles of people who aren’t signed up for its services.
When permissions become real-world harm
This would be scary enough were it not for other stories about Muse privacy invasions. Researcher Patrick Wardle found a way to compromise the software and turn it into a Mac backdoor.
Another team of reporters used it to compile personal details for members of vulnerable groups online. After first declining some of these requests, it capitulated when the prompts were reworded, they said.
Muse also invited a Marketplace buyer to someone’s home last month after accepting a lowball offer on a product that he was selling. Matt Robb, a YouTube tech reviewer, had clicked an “Allow Always” button, assuming that the AI would still ask before sharing his address with strangers. It didn’t. Instead, he said, it arranged the pickup without telling him. The buyer, who traveled half an hour to pick up the product, was not pleased.
If you use Muse, review the accounts it can access, the actions it can take without approval, and whether your interactions are being used for AI training. Give it only the access it needs for the task.

articles.summary:
Meta’s new Muse personal AI agent has surpassed five million downloads while raising significant privacy concerns regarding its extensive data collection and the creation of detailed user dossiers.

### Key Points
- Meta’s Muse AI agent collects up to 31 of 35 data types, including sensitive information like religious beliefs, political opinions, and biometric data.
- Internal instructions reveal the software maintains and refreshes personal dossiers on users and their contacts every hour to track social interactions.
- The app automatically uses user interactions to train Meta’s AI models unless users manually opt out within the application settings.
- Security researchers have identified vulnerabilities, including a potential Mac backdoor and instances where the AI autonomously shared private addresses with strangers.
- Data collected by Muse can include information about non-users who communicate with those who have granted the AI access to their messaging systems.

### Why it Matters
The widespread adoption of Muse highlights the growing tension between AI-driven convenience and the erosion of personal privacy in the digital age. As these agents gain deeper access to private communications and financial accounts, users face increased risks regarding data security and the potential for unauthorized autonomous actions.
